stem: According to the deck's opening definition, 'value' is best understood as:
choices: The perceived benefits that the customer is willing to pay for
The total cost incurred to produce a good or service
The retail price minus the wholesale price
The total revenue generated by a product line
explanation: The deck explicitly rejects a cost-based definition and defines value as the perceived benefit the customer is willing to pay for; cost is a separate term in the margin equation, not value itself.

stem: Per the deck's core identity on value, which equation defines Margin?
choices: Margin = Cost of Creating Value − Value Created
Margin = Value Created − Cost of Creating Value
Margin = Value Created + Cost of Creating Value
explanation: The deck states Margin = Value Created − Cost of Creating Value; raising value or cutting cost both push margin up.

stem: A firm sells Product A at 100 THB/unit (unit cost 60 THB, 500 units sold) and Product B at 80 THB/unit (unit cost 50 THB, 300 units sold). Using Margin = Σ(P_i − C_i) × N_sold_i, what is the firm's total margin?
explanation: Margin sums each product's (price − cost) × quantity: (100−60)×500 = 20,000 plus (80−50)×300 = 9,000, totaling 29,000 THB. 20,000 and 9,000 alone are just the per-product margins, and 74,000 is total revenue, not margin.

stem: The deck asks why Pop Mart doesn't simply raise prices to capture the full margin seen in the resale market. What is the best explanation, given the supply-and-demand diagram on the same slide?
choices: Raising price always increases margin because it increases the per-unit spread (P−C)
Chinese law prohibits toy companies from adjusting prices
Margin only depends on cost, not on price at all
Total margin depends on both the per-unit spread (P−C) and volume sold; a price rise moves the market off equilibrium and can sell fewer units, shrinking total margin
explanation: Margin = Σ(P−C)×N_sold, so it depends on both the spread and the volume sold; the demand curve shows a price increase moves off the equilibrium point and reduces quantity sold, which can shrink total margin even as the per-unit spread grows.

stem: The deck defines the Value Chain as:
choices: The full range of activities a company undertakes (internal operations) to bring a product or service from its initial conception to its end use and beyond
The external flow of goods, materials and information from suppliers to the company to the customer
A tool used to execute specific improvements on time and on budget
The row of Suppliers → Company → Distributors → Users
explanation: This is the deck's definition of the value chain; the other options describe the supply chain (external flow / supplier-to-user row) or project management (delivery tool).

stem: In the deck's diagram, the row 'Suppliers → Company → Distributors → Users' is labeled as:
explanation: The deck labels this row Supply Chain (External Logistics) — the outward-looking external flow of goods, materials and information, distinct from the umbrella value chain above it.

stem: True or False: According to the deck, the supply chain is the broader concept, and the value chain is a part of it.
explanation: It's the reverse — the value chain is the broader, inward-looking umbrella concept, and the supply chain (external logistics) is a part of it.

stem: A retail chain launches a 6-month initiative with a fixed budget and deadline to redesign its warehouse layout and implement the resulting process changes. This initiative itself is best described as an example of:
explanation: Project management 'makes change happen on time and on budget' and is a tool used to improve the value chain or supply chain through structured initiatives — not a rival framework to either.

stem: Which pairing correctly matches each concept with its direction/focus, per the deck?
choices: Value chain – outward looking; Supply chain – inward looking
Value chain – delivery vehicle; Project management – umbrella concept
Supply chain – umbrella concept; Project management – part of the supply chain
Value chain – inward looking (umbrella concept); Supply chain – outward looking (part of the value chain)
explanation: Value chain is inward looking and the umbrella concept; supply chain is outward looking and sits inside the broader value chain; project management is the delivery vehicle for change, not either of these frameworks.

stem: Porter's Value Chain is best described as:
choices: A framework to map out internal activities that add value to your customers
A financial statement summarizing a firm's profit and loss
A project schedule showing task dependencies
A market research tool for measuring customer satisfaction
explanation: The deck defines Porter's Value Chain as a framework to map out internal activities that add value to your customers, visualized as primary activities along the bottom and support activities across the top, with margin as the arrowhead.

stem: Which statement correctly pairs each activity type with the type of competitive advantage it is the source of?
choices: Primary activities → differentiation advantage; Support activities → cost advantage
Primary activities → cost advantage; Support activities → differentiation advantage
Both primary and support activities are sources of cost advantage only
Neither primary nor support activities relate to competitive advantage
explanation: The deck states primary activities directly transform inputs into outputs and are the source of cost advantage, while support activities make primary activities more efficient and are the source of differentiation advantage — getting this reversed is the classic exam trap.

stem: True or False: Primary activities happen in a fixed order, while support activities have no required order.
explanation: Primary activities (Inbound Logistics → Operations → Outbound Logistics → Marketing & Sales → Service) happen in sequence, while support activities have no set order and instead cut across all primary activities.

stem: A Thai food business negotiates and signs a contract with a rice supplier, agreeing on price and delivery terms. This activity belongs to:
explanation: Negotiating and signing the sourcing contract is deciding and acquiring — Procurement. Inbound Logistics only begins once the goods are physically received, stored and moved to where they're used.

stem: A restaurant receives its weekly rice delivery, stores the sacks in a dry warehouse, and moves them into the kitchen as they are needed. Which value chain activity is this?
explanation: Receiving, storing and moving inputs once they are already the firm's own goods is the physical-handling activity of Inbound Logistics, not the deciding-and-acquiring activity of Procurement.

stem: A café builds a custom AI-powered inventory-forecasting dashboard in-house. This activity is:
explanation: Building the analytical tool itself is Technology Development (innovation/R&D/tech tools); Operations would be using an existing tool to run the transformation process, not building it.

stem: The deck notes a wrinkle in Pop Mart's value chain: 3D design & prototyping and quality control (QC) are filed under which activity, even though they might look like R&D?
explanation: For Pop Mart, 3D design & prototyping and QC are the firm's actual transformation step, so the deck classifies them as Operations, while its Technology Development is customer data analytics and digital commerce tech.

stem: In the Pop Mart example, which pair of activities is classified as Technology Development?
choices: Blind box packaging and cross-border logistics
Customer data analytics and digital commerce tech
explanation: Pop Mart's Technology Development covers customer data analytics and digital commerce tech; the 3D design/QC pair sits under Operations, packaging/logistics under Outbound Logistics, and IP acquisition under Procurement.

stem: Starbucks Thailand runs a seasonal 'Thai Tea Frappe' social media campaign to attract new customers. This is:
explanation: Persuading people to buy through campaigns and promotions is Marketing & Sales; Service covers support after the purchase, such as loyalty redemption or the hotline.

stem: A Starbucks Thailand customer redeems loyalty points and calls the customer hotline for help with a mobile-app issue. This is:
explanation: Support after the sale — loyalty redemption and hotline assistance — is Service; Marketing & Sales is about creating awareness and persuading the purchase, not supporting the customer afterward.

stem: Pop Mart signs an IP licensing deal to acquire the rights to a new artist's designs. This is:
explanation: Acquiring the IP and the licensing deal is deciding-and-buying, i.e. Procurement; managing the artist as talent afterward is HRM, and promoting the resulting collaboration is Marketing & Sales — the same artist relationship splits three ways depending on which action is described.

stem: Which Starbucks Thailand activity is correctly classified as Technology Development rather than Outbound Logistics?
choices: Mobile ordering via the Starbucks App
Delivery via GrabFood and LINE MAN
The AI-based inventory and store operations dashboard
explanation: Mobile ordering, delivery via GrabFood/LINE MAN and in-store pickup are all ways the product reaches the customer, i.e. Outbound Logistics; the AI-based inventory/store operations dashboard is the internal tech tool, which is Technology Development.

stem: A company sets up its formal accounting system and office structure. This activity belongs to:
explanation: Company structure, finance, legal and strategy fall under Firm Infrastructure; HRM instead covers hiring, training and retaining people.

stem: Onboarding a new employee and running team training sessions is an example of:
explanation: Hiring, training and retaining people is Human Resource Management, per the deck's support-activities table.

stem: Sourcing fresh ingredients from a new supplier and finding a supplier for packaging materials illustrates:
explanation: Acquiring resources such as raw materials or tools — finding and sourcing suppliers — is Procurement, per the deck's own example.

stem: Select all of the following that are PRIMARY activities in Porter's Value Chain.
explanation: Inbound Logistics, Operations and Marketing & Sales are three of the five primary activities; Firm Infrastructure and Procurement are support activities.

stem: A firm pursuing a cost-leadership strategy would, according to the deck's framework, focus process improvements primarily on:
choices: Support activities, since they are the source of cost advantage
Primary activities, since they are the source of cost advantage
Support activities, since they are the source of differentiation advantage
explanation: The deck states primary activities are the source of cost advantage, so cost-leadership improvements target the primary chain (inbound logistics through service), while differentiation is built through the support activities.

stem: A firm pursuing a differentiation strategy would, per the deck, look to build its advantage primarily through:
explanation: Support activities (Firm Infrastructure, HRM, Technology Development, Procurement) are the deck's stated source of differentiation advantage.

stem: Which statement matches the deck's opening point about value and cost?
choices: Value and cost of production are the same thing
Cost of production always exceeds value created for a profitable firm
Margin is unrelated to either value or cost
Value can be raised without necessarily changing the cost of creating it, since it reflects perceived customer benefit
explanation: Because value is the perceived benefit a customer is willing to pay for — not simply cost — a firm can raise value (e.g. through branding or experience) without changing its cost of creating that value, which raises margin.

stem: The deck notes that Porter's Value Chain was originally designed for what kind of company, and what caveat follows for firms today?
choices: Manufacturing-heavy companies in the 1980s; not all companies need all five primary activities today, and some execute them through partners or platforms
Digital-native startups in the 2010s; all five primary activities are now mandatory
Service companies in the 2020s; support activities are now optional
Financial institutions in the 1990s; primary activities no longer apply
explanation: Porter's framework was designed for manufacturing-heavy companies in the 1980s; the deck notes that value creation today is often digital, decentralized or service-based, so not every company needs all five primary activities and some execute them through partners or platforms.

stem: After mapping out the sub-activities that create value for all primary and support activities, what is the deck's recommended next step in building your own value chain?
choices: Immediately hire a project manager to execute changes
Analyze the sub-activities to make sure each provides more value than its cost
Skip straight to examining linkages among activities without analysis
Raise prices across all primary activities
explanation: The deck's three steps are: (1) map out sub-activities, (2) analyze them to ensure each provides more value than its cost, and (3) examine and optimize the linkages among activities — analysis is the required middle step, not linkage optimization or a price change.

stem: The deck lists four payoffs for building a value chain. Which of the following is one of them?
choices: Eliminating the need for a marketing department
Identifying innovation opportunities — where cost can be reduced, speed improved, or customer experience enhanced
Replacing all support activities with automation
explanation: The deck's four payoffs are: understand how value is created, identify innovation opportunities, drive strategic innovation, and enable cross-functional collaboration; the other options are not listed and misrepresent the framework's purpose.

stem: Manufacturing phones from raw components is an example of which primary activity?
explanation: Transforming inputs into finished products or services — manufacturing phones or cooking meals — is Operations.
